newsitem.title: DENMARK: No Danish rate cut seen despite firm DKK - analysts.
newsitem.headline: No Danish rate cut seen despite firm DKK - analysts.

text.p: Analysts contacted by Reuters on Wednesday ruled out an imminent Danish rate cut despite the growing strength of the crown.
"The fact that the crown has gained in strength against the German mark in the past few days is of no significance," director Mads Jakobsen at Den Danske Bank, Denmark's biggest bank, told Reuters.
"The important fact is that the effective rate against the mark is lower today than it was two years ago," he added.
In recent months the Danish crown has firmed by around one percent against the mark to 3.8140 at Wednesday's close.
This has given rise to market speculation about a possible Danish rate cut.

Jakobsen said he did not see Denmark carrying out an isolated rate cut at this stage. "The Danish Central Bank will be watching both the effective crown rate and its relation to the mark, like the rest of us," he said.
"So long as the crown goes on rising slowly but surely as it is doing at present, it will be a long time before the Danish Central Bank intervenes," Jakobsen said.
He attributed the crown's rise against the mark to the fact that the German currency was losing something of its attraction as the launch of the European single currency approached.
Codan Bank Vice director Niels Lorentz Nielsen said: "The rise of the Danish crown is due to the fundamental strength of Denmark's economy in just about every area."
Currency dealers contacted by Reuters attributed the recent rise in the crown to a major purchase of the currency by the Norwegian Central Bank to deflect upward pressure away from Norway's crown.

"The Norwegian Central Bank's buying up of Danish crowns could well be behind our currency's latest advance. Turnover in the Danish crown has been very low recently," said Frank Fryd Petersen, chief analyst at third biggest BG Bank.

The Danish Central Bank last cut the 14-day certificate of deposit and repurchase rate to 3.50 percent from 3.70 on August 23. It was the ninth trimming of the 14-day rate in 1996. The key deposit rate, cut three times last year, stands at 3.25 percent. Both rates are at historically low levels. --Chris Follett, Copenhagen newsroom +45-33969652
